title: Multi-Agent Orchestration

papers.title: LLM-based Multi-Agents: A Survey of Progress and Challenges

notes.takeaway: Canonical survey of LLM multi-agent systems with the field's reference taxonomy of architectures, coordination patterns, and challenges.
notes.why: The single best entry point; the map every other paper is read against.

papers.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation

notes.takeaway: Introduces the conversable-agent abstraction: agents that send and receive messages, with configurable human and tool participation, composed into flexible conversation patterns.
notes.why: The most-cited framework anchor; its primitives recur in every later vendor SDK (now absorbed into Microsoft Agent Framework).

papers.title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for a Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework

notes.takeaway: Encodes Standard Operating Procedures and a shared message pool so role agents publish structured artifacts (PRDs, designs, code) instead of free chat.
notes.why: Hardened role specialization into an org-chart program; its shared message pool is the lineage of the passive-blackboard team-memory pattern.

papers.title: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate

notes.takeaway: Multiple LLM instances propose, critique, and revise across rounds; factuality and reasoning improve over single-model answers.
notes.why: Origin of the debate-improves-reasoning lineage that later work both extends (sparse topologies) and rebuts (cost of consensus).

papers.title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development

notes.takeaway: Organizes a virtual software company as a chat-chain of phase-scoped two-agent dialogues (design, code, test, document).
notes.why: Society-of-mind made operational; a foundational role-specialization system for software tasks.

papers.title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for Mind Exploration of LLM Society

notes.takeaway: Introduces inception/role-play prompting: an AI-user and an AI-assistant prompt each other into staying on task without human turn-by-turn steering.
notes.why: The oldest role-specialization pattern in the corpus; seeds the autonomous role-play paradigm.

papers.title: AgentVerse: Facilitating Multi-Agent Collaboration and Exploring Emergent Behaviors

notes.takeaway: A framework for assembling collaborating role agents that studies the emergent collaborative behaviors arising when agents work as a group.
notes.why: Early evidence that group dynamics, not just individual capability, shape multi-agent outcomes.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Collaboration: Harnessing the Power of Intelligent LLM Agents

notes.takeaway: A blueprint for coordinating intelligent LLM agents, naming the building blocks of collaboration and control.
notes.why: An early coordination blueprint that frames the design space the topology zoo later fills in.

papers.title: Dynamic LLM-Powered Agent Network for Task-Oriented Agent Collaboration (DyLAN)

notes.takeaway: Activates and connects agents dynamically based on the task rather than a fixed wiring, with an inference-time agent-importance score for team selection.
notes.why: The corpus anchor for dynamic topology / routing — the precursor to adaptive, query-conditioned orchestration.

papers.title: Improving Multi-Agent Debate with Sparse Communication Topology

notes.takeaway: Shows that all-to-all debate is wasteful: a sparse communication topology preserves most of the reasoning benefit at a fraction of the token cost.
notes.why: The standing rebuttal to dense-debate defaults; couples topology choice to cost directly.

papers.title: Magentic-One: A Generalist Multi-Agent System for Solving Complex Tasks

notes.takeaway: Reference orchestrator-worker architecture: a lead Orchestrator maintains task and progress ledgers, dispatches to specialist workers (web surfer, coder, file navigator), and re-plans when stuck.
notes.why: The canonical production topology and the ledger pattern that defines shared working state in a team.

papers.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)

notes.takeaway: First systematic 14-category taxonomy of why multi-agent systems fail, built by hand-annotating real traces; failures span specification, inter-agent misalignment, and verification.
notes.why: Gives the field named failure modes and shows most production breakage is coordination, not base-model cognition.

papers.title: MALT: Improving Reasoning with Multi-Agent LLM Training

notes.takeaway: Trains specialized generator, verifier, and refiner roles jointly rather than relying on prompted role-play.
notes.why: Pushes role specialization from prompting toward trained division of labor.

papers.title: MACI: Multi-Agent Collaborative Intelligence for Adaptive Reasoning and Temporal Planning

notes.takeaway: A meta-planner coordinates collaborative agents for adaptive reasoning and temporal planning over constraints.
notes.why: Treats planning itself as a coordinated meta-layer rather than a single agent's job.

papers.title: S-Agents: Self-organizing Agents in Open-ended Environments

notes.takeaway: Self-organizes agents into a tree-of-agents structure for open-ended environments without a fixed central controller.
notes.why: A swarm/decentralized point in the topology zoo; coordination emerges from local structure.

papers.title: Hierarchical Language Agent for Real-time Human-AI Coordination

notes.takeaway: A hierarchical agent architecture that meets real-time latency constraints in human-AI coordination.
notes.why: Shows hierarchy as a lever for latency and responsiveness, not just organizational tidiness.

papers.title: DynTaskMAS: Dynamic Task-Graph LLM Multi-Agent System

notes.takeaway: Decomposes work into an asynchronous task-graph so independent sub-tasks run in parallel rather than in a serial chat.
notes.why: Moves orchestration from chat sequences toward true parallel dataflow.

papers.title: AgentNet: Decentralized Evolutionary Coordination for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: A decentralized scheme where agents evolve their connections over time, adapting the coordination graph without central control.
notes.why: An evolutionary take on decentralized topology — the network learns its own wiring.

papers.title: Coordination as an Architectural Layer for LLM Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: Argues coordination should be a first-class architectural layer rather than an emergent side effect of prompting.
notes.why: Names the design move the whole field is converging on: make coordination explicit and inspectable.

papers.title: Cayley Graph Optimization for Scalable MAS Communication Topologies

notes.takeaway: Uses Cayley-graph structure to design communication topologies that scale efficiently as agent count grows.
notes.why: A principled, mathematically-grounded approach to the topology-scalability problem.

papers.title: A Two-Dimensional Framework for AI Agent Design Patterns

notes.takeaway: Organizes the space of agent design patterns along two axes, producing a structured pattern taxonomy.
notes.why: The right citation for 'here is the map of all the patterns' — a modern pattern catalogue.

papers.title: TraceFix: Repairing Agent Coordination Protocols with TLA+

notes.takeaway: Models an agent coordination protocol in TLA+ and automatically finds and repairs coordination bugs the way model checkers find deadlocks in distributed protocols.
notes.why: The most direct import of classical formal methods; partial answer to 'can we prove a handoff is safe.'

papers.title: MPAC: Multi-Principal Agent Coordination Protocol

notes.takeaway: A multi-principal coordination layer that sits above tool/messaging protocols like MCP and A2A to coordinate agents serving different principals.
notes.why: Addresses interoperability and trust when agents answer to multiple owners.

papers.title: ARIADNE: Blackboard-Driven Monte-Carlo Tree Search for Multi-Agent Reasoning

notes.takeaway: Drives a Monte-Carlo tree search over a shared blackboard that agents read and write rather than messaging each other directly.
notes.why: A modern instantiation of the classic blackboard/shared-workspace architecture; sits on the passive-substrate side of the team-memory debate.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems via Decentralized Memory

notes.takeaway: Fuses agent-memory and MAS: persistent decentralized team state lets a multi-agent system self-evolve, weighing shared versus per-agent memory.
notes.why: Directly bridges the agentic-memory and multi-agent series — team state as the substrate of self-improvement.

papers.title: SHIMI: Semantic Hierarchical Memory Index for Collective Agent Memory

notes.takeaway: A semantic hierarchical memory index used as collective memory, synchronized across nodes via a Merkle-DAG + CRDT scheme so the shared store converges without a central coordinator.
notes.why: Shows collective memory can be both structured and decentralized-consistent at once.

papers.title: iAgents: Collaborative Task Completion under Information Asymmetry

notes.takeaway: Studies what each agent knows versus what it must communicate when information is asymmetrically distributed across a team.
notes.why: Reframes communication as the explicit transfer of privately-held knowledge — a core team-memory question.

papers.title: DroidSpeak: KV Cache Sharing for Cross-LLM Communication

notes.takeaway: When agents share a base model, KV caches can be shared across them to cut cross-LLM communication cost — shared memory at the attention-state level.
notes.why: The lowest, most literal tier of shared memory; trades text-passing for substrate-level state.

papers.title: LCGuard: Safe KV Cache Sharing in Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: Treats shared KV-cache representations as an attack surface and guards them, the safety counterweight to DroidSpeak-style sharing.
notes.why: Shows that the cheapest shared-memory tier is also a new security boundary.

papers.title: IBGP: Imperfect Byzantine Generals Problem for Multi-Agent Robustness

notes.takeaway: Frames error propagation in agent teams as an imperfect Byzantine-generals consensus problem.
notes.why: Imports classical fault-tolerance theory to reason about how bad outputs spread and can be contained.

papers.title: ACIArena: Evaluating Agent Cascading Injection

notes.takeaway: A benchmark for agent cascading injection — how an injected instruction propagates through shared context from one agent to the next.
notes.why: Quantifies error/attack propagation via the shared substrate, the dark side of team memory.

papers.title: Aligned Agents, Biased Swarm: Bias Amplification in Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: Shows individually aligned agents can produce a biased swarm: bias is amplified through memory-mediated interaction even when each agent is fine.
notes.why: Refutes any deployment story built on 'each agent is individually safe'; per-agent alignment does not compose.

papers.title: Topology and Memory of Consensus among LLM Agents

notes.takeaway: Studies how communication topology and agent memory jointly shape whether a team reaches consensus.
notes.why: Makes explicit that memory and topology interact — neither can be tuned in isolation.

papers.title: The Dynamics of Social Conventions in LLM Populations

notes.takeaway: Documents how social conventions emerge from accumulated interaction memory in populations of LLM agents.
notes.why: Evidence that norms precipitate out of a shared memory substrate over time.

papers.title: Spontaneous Emergence of Agent Individuality through Social Interactions in LLM-Based Communities

notes.takeaway: Distinct agent identities emerge spontaneously from accumulated interaction memory in LLM communities.
notes.why: Identity, like convention, is shown to be a downstream product of memory accumulation.

papers.title: Agent Workflow Memory

notes.takeaway: Distills reusable procedural routines (workflows) from past trajectories so agents stop re-deriving the same multi-step procedures.
notes.why: Seeds the procedural/workflow tier of team memory that later shared-repo systems scale across users.

papers.title: Encouraging Divergent Thinking in LLMs through Multi-Agent Debate

notes.takeaway: Uses multi-agent debate to counter the degeneration-of-thought problem and encourage divergent reasoning.
notes.why: A high-citation debate result showing communication itself is a coordination mechanism against premature convergence.

papers.title: ReConcile: Round-Table Conference Improves Reasoning via Consensus among Diverse LLMs

notes.takeaway: A round-table consensus protocol among diverse LLMs that share deliberation and revise toward agreement.
notes.why: An early structured-consensus method and shared-deliberation-memory pattern.

papers.title: AutoGen Studio: A No-Code Developer Tool for Building and Debugging Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: A no-code tool for building, debugging, and inspecting multi-agent message flow and state on top of AutoGen.
notes.why: Tooling for the message-flow/state layer — making coordination observable to builders.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies

notes.takeaway: Jointly optimizes prompts and communication topologies, showing topology is a first-class lever on performance, not a deployment afterthought.
notes.why: Independent corroboration that the wiring, held model fixed, drives outcomes.

papers.title: Decentralized Generative Agents with Adaptive Hierarchical Knowledge Graph

notes.takeaway: Maintains a shared, adaptive hierarchical knowledge graph as collective memory so structured facts persist and compose across agents.
notes.why: A structured-knowledge tier of team memory — collective memory as a queryable graph.

papers.title: Project Sid: Many-Agent Simulations toward AI Civilization

notes.takeaway: Scales generative agents to many-agent civilization simulations with institutional memory: laws, roles, and culture that persist beyond any one agent.
notes.why: The institutional-memory tier — conventions and identity at population scale.

papers.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior

notes.takeaway: Establishes the memory-stream-plus-reflection architecture: agents record observations, retrieve by relevance/recency/importance, and synthesize higher-level reflections.
notes.why: The memory anchor of the whole field and the crossover point with the agentic-memory series; believable society from memory alone.

papers.title: Emergent Communication in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Enhances Foraging

notes.takeaway: Pre-LLM result: emergent communication via stigmergy enhances collective foraging in multi-agent RL.
notes.why: Roots externalized, environment-mediated coordination (stigmergy) that LLM swarms re-instantiate.

papers.title: PheroCom: Virtual Pheromone-based Communication for Swarm Coordination

notes.takeaway: Coordinates a swarm through virtual pheromones — externalized collective memory written into a shared field.
notes.why: A classic externalized-memory coordination mechanism; ancestor of blackboard/shared-field designs.

papers.title: Robust Multi-Agent LLMs under Byzantine Faults

notes.takeaway: Studies and improves reliability of multi-agent LLM systems when some agents are Byzantine-faulty (arbitrarily wrong or adversarial).
notes.why: Brings distributed-systems fault tolerance to agent teams as a reliability discipline.

papers.title: From Debate to Decision: Conformal Social Choice for Multi-Agent Consensus

notes.takeaway: Applies conformal prediction to multi-agent consensus, giving a principled abstention threshold so the system can decline rather than ratify confidently-wrong agreement.
notes.why: Separates agreement from correctness — a foundation for calibrated consensus and safe abstention.

papers.title: Governance by Construction for Generalist Agents

notes.takeaway: Compiles policy-as-code with human-in-the-loop checkpoints so governance is built into the agent's execution path by construction.
notes.why: Operationalizes governance as a compile-time/runtime guarantee rather than a review afterthought.

papers.title: AGrail: A Lifelong Agent Guardrail with Effective and Adaptive Safety Detection

notes.takeaway: A lifelong, adaptive runtime guardrail that updates its safety detection over the agent's operational lifetime.
notes.why: Moves guardrails from static filters to adaptive, continuously-learning runtime controls.

papers.title: Current State of LLM Risks and AI Guardrails

notes.takeaway: Surveys LLM risks and the landscape of AI guardrail techniques.
notes.why: A reference map of the guardrail design space production teams draw from.

papers.title: Prompt Infection: LLM-to-LLM Prompt Injection within Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: Demonstrates agent-to-agent prompt injection: a malicious instruction launders itself through one agent's output into another's input.
notes.why: Names the core multi-agent attack — the architecture itself becomes the attack surface.

papers.title: Agent Security Bench (ASB): Formalizing and Benchmarking Attacks and Defenses in LLM-based Agents

notes.takeaway: A benchmark formalizing attacks and defenses across the LLM-agent attack surface (prompt injection, memory poisoning, tool misuse).
notes.why: Gives the field a shared yardstick for agent security claims.

papers.title: A Reward Hacking Benchmark for Tool-Use Agents

notes.takeaway: Benchmarks spec-gaming / reward hacking in tool-use agents — agents satisfying the letter of a goal while violating intent.
notes.why: Targets the silent failure where an agent's tool call is syntactically perfect but semantically wrong.

papers.title: CodeTracer: Traceable Agent States for Debugging

notes.takeaway: Makes agent states traceable so multi-agent runs can be reconstructed and debugged step by step.
notes.why: The research counterpart to OpenTelemetry's operational standard for replayable agent traces.

papers.title: Acceptance-Test-Driven Evaluation Protocols for Agents

notes.takeaway: Proposes acceptance-test-driven evaluation protocols for enterprise agents, replacing ad hoc demos with pre-agreed pass/fail criteria.
notes.why: Brings software-engineering acceptance testing to agent evaluation — the basis for 'earned autonomy' thresholds.

papers.title: CompliBench: LLM Judges for Compliance Violation Detection

notes.takeaway: A benchmark for using LLM judges to detect compliance violations in agent behavior.
notes.why: Targets the compliance-guardrail evaluation gap for regulated deployments.

papers.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP): Landscape, Security Threats, and Future Directions

notes.takeaway: Surveys the MCP tool-integration protocol landscape and its security threats (tool poisoning, confused-deputy, supply-chain risk).
notes.why: The corpus anchor for the tool-integration substrate every agent stack now depends on.

papers.title: CascadeDebate: Cost-Aware LLM Cascades for Multi-Agent Debate

notes.takeaway: Cost-aware cascades that escalate to expensive models only when cheaper ones disagree, controlling debate's compute blow-up.
notes.why: A direct attack on the cost axis of orchestration via cognitive-tier routing.

papers.title: ATOM: Adaptive Nucleus-Electron Orchestration for Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: An adaptive orchestrator with a stable offline-learned nucleus and query-conditioned worker electrons activated only when difficulty warrants; names the 'average-complexity trap' of static dense topologies.
notes.why: Shows topology should bend to task difficulty — up to 30% token savings by right-sizing the team per query.

papers.title: Predictive Maps of Multi-Agent Reasoning: Spectral Diagnostics of Topology

notes.takeaway: Derives closed-form spectra of the communication operator that map to three failure modes, giving a pre-deployment diagnostic of a topology.
notes.why: Reframes 'pick a topology' from taste to engineering: condition number, spectral gap, and radius predict robustness, consensus, and drift.

papers.title: Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration (MacNet)

notes.takeaway: Organizes 1000+ agents as a directed acyclic graph and finds a collaborative scaling law: performance follows a logistic growth curve, with irregular topologies beating regular ones (chain, star, tree, complete).
notes.why: The optimist pole of the scaling debate; collaborative emergence appears earlier than neural-scaling emergence.

papers.title: Scaling Behavior of Single LLM-Driven Multi-Agent Systems (SIMAS)

notes.takeaway: Isolates the effect of adding agents from model/knowledge heterogeneity and finds MAS performance does not scale monotonically — diminishing returns governed by a synergy-versus-coordination-overhead trade-off.
notes.why: The pessimist pole of the scaling debate; collective intelligence is contingent on interaction design, not agent count.

papers.title: Embodied LLM Agents Learn to Cooperate in Organized Teams

notes.takeaway: Flat LLM teams over-report and over-comply, creating redundancy and confusion; imposing prompt-based organizational structure with designated leadership improves efficiency and cuts communication cost.
notes.why: Empirical case that hierarchy is a lever to suppress chatter, not just an org-chart box.

papers.title: MMA2A: Multi-Modal Agent-to-Agent Routing and the Information Topology

notes.takeaway: On CrossModal-CS, modality-native routing reached 52% task completion vs 32% for a text-bottleneck baseline with the same backend — but only when an LLM (not keyword matching) consumed the richer context.
notes.why: The sharpest ablation in the corpus: the pattern, not the model, is the variable, and richer protocols buy nothing without a reasoning layer that can exploit them.

papers.title: Agents in Software Engineering: Survey, Landscape, and Vision

notes.takeaway: Surveys SE agents with a clean perception / memory / action three-module mental model for what each role agent is.
notes.why: The cleanest abstraction for reasoning about a role agent before naming any framework.

papers.title: OpenHands: An Open Platform for AI Software Developers as Generalist Agents

notes.takeaway: A generalist code-agent platform (formerly OpenDevin) with explicit multi-agent coordination and sandboxed execution.
notes.why: The bridge from coordination patterns to systems developers actually run.

papers.title: SOEN-101 / FlowGen: Code Generation via Software-Process Models with Multi-Agent

notes.takeaway: Instantiates Waterfall, TDD, and Scrum as multi-agent topologies with the same role agents re-wired into different communication patterns, yielding different code quality.
notes.why: The vivid demonstration that the org chart is literally the program.

papers.title: Beyond Individual Intelligence: The LIFE Progression of Multi-Agent Capability

notes.takeaway: A LIFE-progression taxonomy (Lay capability, Integrate, Find faults, Evolve) that unifies collaboration, failure-attribution, and self-evolution into one structural arc.
notes.why: Gives the maturity arc a vocabulary — from doing the task to evolving the team.

papers.title: OneManCompany: Dynamically Recruited Agent Workforces from a Talent Market

notes.takeaway: Packages skills, tools, and config into portable 'Talent' identities recruited on demand from a Talent Market, decoupling org structure from what an agent knows.
notes.why: Fixed crews give way to dynamically recruited workforces — org as a separate, governable concern.

papers.title: Theater of Mind for LLMs: From Blackboard to the Global Workspace

notes.takeaway: A naive two-agent loop over a passive shared pool rapidly descends into cognitive stagnation; Global Workspace Agents replace polling with an active broadcast hub, an entropy-based diversity drive, and bifurcated short-term/long-term memory.
notes.why: The hinge result for team memory: passive sharing fails; memory must be actively broadcast, curated, and consolidated.

papers.title: SkillClaw: Shared Synchronized Workflow Memory across a Multi-User Agent Ecosystem

notes.takeaway: Aggregates cross-user trajectories into a shared, synchronized workflow-memory repo; an autonomous evolver turns recurring patterns into skill refinements that propagate system-wide.
notes.why: Stops workflows and failure modes from being repeatedly rediscovered per user — procedural memory at ecosystem scale.

papers.title: M*: Every Task Deserves Its Own Memory Harness

notes.takeaway: Argues a memory system optimized for one purpose fails to transfer, and uses reflective code-evolution to auto-discover a task-specialized memory program (Schema + Logic + Instructions).
notes.why: The contrarian counterweight to one-shared-substrate: per-task specialization as a live, unsolved design axis.

papers.title: Governance by Design: A Parsonian Institutional Audit of an Agent Ecosystem

notes.takeaway: A Parsonian governance audit of a large agent ecosystem (250k+ stars, 770k+ agents, 2M+ users) finds <=19% governance coverage and zero of twelve coordination pathways functional.
notes.why: Macro-scale rebuttal to 'conventions emerge automatically'; shared substrate is necessary but not sufficient without governance.

papers.title: Auto-Dreamer: CLS-based Fast Acquisition and Slow Consolidation of Agent Memory

notes.takeaway: Invokes Complementary Learning Systems theory to decouple fast per-session memory acquisition from slow cross-session consolidation; a learned offline consolidator synthesizes compact replacements that supersede bloated regions.
notes.why: Makes records-management-as-consolidation executable: +7 on ScienceWorld with a 12x smaller memory bank, transferring without retraining.

papers.title: Unified Context Evolution (UCE): A Typed Library of Evolvable Context Units

notes.takeaway: A gradient-free typed library of Evolvable Context Units (Memory, Strategy, Workflow, Skill), each generated from trajectories, quality-scored through use, and pruned when no longer valuable.
notes.why: Records-management governance for a team substrate: typing + quality tracking + retention carry the gains (ALFWorld 75.4%->96.3%).

papers.title: Architecture Matters: Security in Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: Across three environments and 13 configurations, multi-agent setups were more vulnerable than single agents in most configs, with attack-success rates varying up to 3.8x at equal-or-higher benign accuracy; no design was universally safer.
notes.why: Kills the intuition that decomposition is inherently a defense — the architecture itself is the security variable.

papers.title: Cross-Session Threats: Memoryless Guardrails in Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: An attacker who spreads a single attack across dozens of sessions evades every session-bound detector; session judges and full-log correlators lose ~half their recall, recovered by a bounded Coreset Memory Reader (K=50).
notes.why: Shows guardrails must be stateful across sessions, not just within one; releases CSTM-Bench.

papers.title: Context-Fragmented Policy Violations in Multi-Agent Workflows

notes.takeaway: Each agent's action is locally safe but the actions collectively violate policy because policy facts are siloed across departments; eight frontier LLMs showed 14-98% violation rates, and a Distributed Sentinel with Semantic Taint Tokens reached F1=0.95 at 106 ms.
notes.why: Formalizes the confused-deputy export incident; guardrails must be distributed and zero-trust, not a monolithic gate.

papers.title: GAMMAF: Graph-based Anomaly Monitoring of Multi-Agent Debates

notes.takeaway: Models MAS debates as attributed graphs and benchmarks graph-based anomaly detectors that isolate flagged adversarial nodes live.
notes.why: Bridges security and observability — treats the interaction graph itself as the monitored signal.

papers.title: The Cost of Consensus: When Multi-Agent Debate Underperforms Self-Correction

notes.takeaway: Isolated self-correction beats unguided homogeneous multi-agent debate: debate fails via sycophantic conformity (up to 85.5%), contextual fragility (up to 70%), and consensus collapse (oracle gap up to 32.3 pp).
notes.why: The sharpest dissent against the multi-agent reflex; directly undercuts the debate-improves-reasoning lineage.

papers.title: Liability and Accountability for AI Agents: A Principal-Agent Perspective

notes.takeaway: Frames the accountability question — who is responsible when the agent is wrong — through a principal-agent lens.
notes.why: Motivates interpretability, behavior evals, and fail-safe mechanisms as governance instruments.

papers.title: Bounded Autonomy for Enterprise AI

notes.takeaway: Typed action contracts, consumer-side execution, validation-before-side-effects, and optional human approval in a deployed multi-tenant app: 23/25 trials with zero unsafe executions vs 17/25 unconstrained, both at 13-18x speedup.
notes.why: The standout production-deployment result; two wrong-entity mutations escaped every automated layer and were caught only by human confirmation.

papers.title: Pioneer Agent: Closed-Loop Continual Improvement of Small Models in Production

notes.takeaway: Closed-loop continual improvement of small models in production via automated data curation, failure diagnosis, and regression-constrained retraining (AdaptFT-Bench).
notes.why: Attacks the cost axis from the model side — supports SLM routing without regressions.

papers.title: Token Budgets: An Empirical Catalog and Affine-Typed Mitigation of Orchestration Cost Overruns

notes.takeaway: Catalogs 63 confirmed production budget-overrun incidents across 21 orchestration frameworks into an 8-cluster taxonomy, and ships a Rust crate using affine ownership so double-spending a budget becomes a compile error.
notes.why: Moves cost control from a code-review comment into the type system; non-bypassable under operator error in multi-agent delegation.

papers.title: AgentForesight: Online Auditing for Early Failure Prediction in Agent Trajectories

notes.takeaway: Reframes failure attribution as online auditing: a 7B auditor sees only the current trajectory prefix and must let the run continue or raise an alarm at the earliest decisive error.
notes.why: Shifts attribution from diagnose-after-death to intervene-while-alive; beats GPT-4.1 by up to +19.9% with 3x lower step-localization error.

papers.title: HORIZON: A Cross-Domain Diagnostic Benchmark for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks

notes.takeaway: A diagnostic benchmark of 3,100+ trajectories from GPT-5 and Claude variants with a trajectory-grounded LLM-as-judge characterizing where and why long-horizon agentic tasks break.
notes.why: The empirical substrate for causal failure attribution at scale.

papers.title: HARBOR: Harness Tuning as Constrained Bayesian Optimization

notes.takeaway: Argues the harness (compaction, tool caching, memory, trajectory reuse) is a first-class ML problem and formalizes harness tuning as constrained noisy Bayesian optimization over a mixed-variable config space.
notes.why: Automated search beats hand-tuned flag stacks once the configuration space exceeds a few bits.

papers.title: The Capability Paradox: Stronger Workers, Less Secure Systems

notes.takeaway: Across 42,000 adversarial trials, stronger Worker agents made the system less secure (ASR 18.4%->63.9%, peak 94.4%); linguistic certainty mediates 74% of the effect via 'semantic hijacking.'
notes.why: Refutes 'use a smarter model'; confidence is weaponized, and a heterogeneous-ensemble defense cuts ASR from 52.8% to 2.0%.

papers.title: Knowing When Not to Answer: Abstention in Multi-Agent VLM Systems (MM-AQA)

notes.takeaway: Benchmarks abstention (MM-AQA) and finds VLMs rarely abstain under standard prompting — even trivial confidence baselines beat them; multi-agent setups improve abstention but introduce new failure modes.
notes.why: Concrete evidence for the confidence-is-not-correctness thread in calibrated consensus.

papers.title: GSAR: Grounded Consensus via Typed Claim Grounding for Hallucination Detection

notes.takeaway: Operationalizes grounded consensus with a 4-way claim typology (grounded/ungrounded/contradicted/complementary), evidence-type-specific weights, and an asymmetric contradiction-penalized groundedness score driving a 3-tier replan decision.
notes.why: A concrete mechanism for separating confidence from correctness in team deliberation.

papers.title: SWARM: Soft-Label Population-Level Governance for Emergent Multi-Agent Risk

notes.takeaway: Replaces binary good/bad labels with soft probabilistic labels and adds governance levers (transaction taxes, circuit breakers, reputation decay, random audits) measured by expected-toxicity and quality-gap metrics over multi-seed scenarios.
notes.why: Evaluates the swarm, not the agent — targets risks no single agent produces in isolation.

papers.title: AMBIPOM: How to Steer Your Multi-Agent System (Human-LLM Co-Planning)

notes.takeaway: Formalizes a human-LLM co-planning design space along three axes (mode, scope, level) and shifts supervision from outcome-level to process-level.
notes.why: A principled framework for optimal human-checkpoint placement in the loop.

papers.title: Triage: Routing Software Engineering Tasks to Cost-Effective LLM Tiers via Code Quality Signals

notes.takeaway: Cost-tier routing for SWE tasks — closest single paper to the Gas City tiering problem.
notes.why: Surfaced by the 2026-06-11 dense-lane rerun (missed in the lexical-only window).

papers.title: A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs

notes.takeaway: Unifies routing + cascading formally.
notes.why: Surfaced by the 2026-06-11 dense-lane rerun (missed in the lexical-only window).

papers.title: EMAFusion: A Self-Optimizing System for Seamless LLM Selection and Integration

notes.takeaway: Self-optimizing LLM selection.
notes.why: Surfaced by the 2026-06-11 dense-lane rerun (missed in the lexical-only window).

papers.title: Agreement-Based Cascading for Efficient Inference

notes.takeaway: Cascade via inter-model agreement.
notes.why: Surfaced by the 2026-06-11 dense-lane rerun (missed in the lexical-only window).

papers.title: Cascade-Aware Training of Language Models

notes.takeaway: Trains models with the cascade in mind.

papers.title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Shared Context (DeLM)

notes.takeaway: Replaces centralized scatter-gather orchestration — a main agent assigns subtasks, waits, and merges — with decentralized coordination: parallel agents asynchronously claim tasks from a shared queue and read/write a shared verified context, removing the central merge/broadcast bottleneck.
notes.why: The foundations branch's topology question: DeLM argues centralized MAS parallelize execution but not coordination, and that a shared-state topology scales better as subtask count grows.

notes.takeaway: The shared context is the communication substrate: agents write compact verified gists (coarse-to-fine 'unfoldable' — expand to detailed summaries or raw evidence only when needed), and each update is checked against its evidence at admission time so unsupported claims are rejected before becoming reusable problem state.
notes.why: The memory-in-MAS branch's exact concern — the shared substrate a team writes to and who governs it; DeLM's admission-time verification is the governance mechanism keeping shared memory trustworthy.

notes.takeaway: On SWE-bench Verified DeLM reaches 77.4% pass@4 at ~$0.12/task (roughly half the baselines' cost); on LongBench-v2 Multi-Doc QA it leads four frontier model families by up to 5.7 points, with both admission-time verification and hierarchical summarization contributing.
notes.why: The production branch's reliability/cost axis — a decentralized topology that improves accuracy while cutting cost.

papers.title: XFlow: An Executable Protocol Programming System for Reliable Multi-Agent Workflows

notes.takeaway: XFlow positions existing frameworks on a Chomsky-hierarchy spectrum: markup/config frameworks (LangGraph as graphs) describe workflow shape but leave the prompt-harness boundary undefined; conversation-centric (AutoGen) and role/task frameworks (CrewAI's teams/tasks/crews/flows) push coordination into agent dialogue. XPF instead re-encodes the recurring coordination primitives explicitly as compilable structures: symbols (typed state cells), actor interfaces with read/write sets, control flow (guarded goto/call for loops, retries, escalation), and responsibility transfer (handoff blocks guarded by predicates).
notes.why: Names the small shared vocabulary every framework re-encodes (state, actor I/O contracts, guarded transitions, handoffs) and shows a concrete proposal for lifting it out of prompts into a checkable, compiled interop layer rather than free-form text.

notes.takeaway: On tau3-bench, XFlow raises constraint-compliance to 100% in Retail/Airline (from 96.5%/91.8%) with Qwen3.5-9B and to 100% across all three DeepSeek-V4-Flash domains (Telecom +36.3pp) while holding task pass1, decoupling correctness from compliance. CorpusQA accuracy +2.4 (Qwen) to 61.7 and +0.9 to 75.7 (DeepSeek); SWE-bench Verified pass rate 77.4 to 79.8 (+2.4) over mini-SWE-agent. Reliability is enforced by a verified compile step (static checks on symbols, stage targets, schema/call bindings) plus runtime lifecycle gating of state commits.
notes.why: Adds a named system (XFlow/XPF) to the reliability reckoning with concrete deltas on three benchmark classes, and grounds the gain in verified protocol structure rather than a better prompt.

papers.title: Knowledge-Based Zero-Replay Debugging of Multi-Agent LLM Traces

notes.takeaway: Named system BranchPoint-Latent reframes causal attribution in multi-agent traces as zero-replay counterfactual-effect prediction: predict which events a counterfactual-replay oracle would mark high-effect before any replay is run. A gradient-boosted learning-to-rank predictor over 13 knowledge-graph features lifts Branch Recall@5 from 0.73 to 0.95 in-distribution and 0.93 on held-out families, per-trace rho from 0.47 to 0.80/0.77, all at zero oracle-replay cost (CPU milliseconds per trace vs seconds-to-minutes per GPU replay call, an explicit O(T*|F|*N) baseline). No single selector dominates: the learned predictor wins tool/latent-dominant traces (MBPP 1.00 vs centrality 0.00) while centrality matches or beats it on graph-dominant chains, and a structural router does not beat the always-learned default.
notes.why: A 2026 reliability-reckoning paper with a named system hitting exactly the frontier axes: causal attribution (replay oracle ground truth), explicit cost bounds, and regime-dependent behavior, while refusing to over-claim about where cheap structural signals already suffice.

papers.title: ESAA-Conversational: An Event-Sourced Memory Layer for Continuity, Handoff, and Curation Across Heterogeneous LLM Coding Agents

notes.takeaway: The shared substrate is a single append-only event log written by all agents, with workspace_root as a mandatory isolation boundary and agent_id tagging each turn. Conventions (handoff.md, decisions.md) and identity precipitate out as deterministic projections; a cold agent enters through handoff.md plus a paginated context window rather than the full log.
notes.why: A worked example of the shared-memory substrate for an agent team — governance (workspace isolation, a single-writer lockfile, the append-only contract) and identity are built into the event schema itself.

papers.title: The Red Queen Gödel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators

notes.takeaway: Extends Gödel-machine-style recursive self-improvement to non-stationary utilities: each archive node is a multi-agent workspace holding task agents and learned evaluators that co-evolve, with Thompson sampling over clade metaproductivity steering the search. Co-evolved writers reach 1.78–1.86× higher paper-acceptance rates under a diverse judge panel and a co-evolved grader reaches 9% higher ground-truth accuracy than static baselines.
notes.why: A named system with real numbers for the co-evolution frontier: evaluation itself becomes an evolving component of the agent system, with convergence guarantees held per epoch rather than abandoned.

papers.title: Govern the Repository, Not the Agent: Measuring Ecosystem-Level Risk in AI-Native Software

notes.takeaway: The paper measures 'statistical non-reducibility' with multilevel models the field already uses, and validates the agent-specific signal against a matched human-authored baseline in the same repositories.
notes.why: A practical, metric-independent method production teams can reuse to test whether their repos are absorbing agent-driven friction beyond what any single-agent benchmark would predict.

papers.title: Glite ARF: Verifier-Driven Research with Parallel LLM Coding Agents

notes.takeaway: Deployed across three research campaigns including a BEA 2026 shared-task submission (first and second place) run by up to twelve parallel coding agents from a single laptop at ~$450 in API spend, with the framework's verification and isolation machinery adding only ~1% wall-clock overhead.
notes.why: Real cost and overhead numbers for running many parallel coding agents against a shared repository, useful evidence for routing and cost tradeoffs around structural guardrails.

notes.takeaway: Glite ARF is explicitly orthogonal to intra-task orchestration frameworks (AutoGen, MetaGPT, CrewAI): it wraps the campaign-level lifecycle (task isolation, immutable artifacts, verifier scripts) around whichever framework runs inside a single task.
notes.why: Names a coordination layer, a verifier-driven, spec-enforced task lifecycle, distinct from intra-task multi-agent frameworks, a pattern this branch tracks.

papers.title: WebSwarm: Recursive Multi-Agent Orchestration for Deep-and-Wide Web Search

notes.takeaway: WebSwarm replaces root-only task decomposition with progressive recursive delegation: the root agent instantiates search nodes as intermediate evidence reveals new subgoals, each node either solves its objective directly or spawns and coordinates child nodes, and results flow back up so a parent can expand, revise, or aggregate. On BrowseComp-Plus this deep-and-wide topology beats a single ReAct agent by 17.50 accuracy points, and an ablation removing recursive delegation drops BrowseComp-Plus accuracy from 68.00 to 63.50.
notes.why: This branch asks what a multi-agent system is as a topology and when structure beats one long trajectory; WebSwarm's answer is that the decomposition tree should be built as evidence accumulates rather than fixed upfront, and it measures that against single-agent and fixed-decomposition baselines.

notes.takeaway: Each node carries a search mode that selects its local collaboration pattern from a small vocabulary, parallel divide-and-conquer, sequential search-and-verification, or multi-path sampling and aggregation, rather than imposing one global paradigm across the task. A lightweight web-probing step first checks whether the needed evidence sits in a few hub pages or is spread along a dimension, and that signal decides how a node expands; removing web-probing inflates average web-tool calls (for example from 137.03 to 239.90 in one setting), so it mainly cuts redundant search.
notes.why: This branch tracks the recurring coordination patterns frameworks re-encode; WebSwarm's contribution is making the pattern a per-node choice conditioned on how the web organizes the needed evidence, instead of a single fixed collaboration structure.

papers.title: Learning Latency-Aware Orchestration for Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: End-to-end latency in a multi-agent system is set by the critical execution path, the longest chain of dependent operators, not by the summed cost across all operators. LAMaS makes that structural fact the training signal: it minimizes E[lambda_t*T + lambda_c*C] subject to an accuracy floor E[S] >= S0, solved by Lagrangian relaxation whose dual variable rises when accuracy slips below the floor and relaxes when it holds. Credit is weighted per operator by path-criticality w(o) = l(o)/T, so bottleneck operators absorb the full latency penalty and off-path operators get effectively none. A second, lightweight MLP controller runs at inference and cuts redundant remaining agent calls once operator outputs already agree. Against MaAS, GDesigner and AgentDropout on GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH and MMLU-Pro with gpt-4o-mini, LAMaS cuts end-to-end latency 55.6-75.6% while matching or beating accuracy (GSM8K: 11.73s vs MaAS 48.11s at 93.65% vs 93.36%). The pipeline transfers: GDesigner+LAMaS drops GSM8K latency from 32.31s to 20.55s at unchanged accuracy.
notes.why: This branch covers the runtime properties that decide whether an orchestrated system survives deployment, and latency is the one automated-orchestration work has mostly folded into cost. The paper shows the two objectives diverge structurally, and its ablation prices the naive fix: bolting a uniform latency term onto the reward costs 1.30-5.34 accuracy points for only 2-11% latency savings, while the critical-path-aware version with an explicit accuracy floor keeps accuracy and takes the full reduction.

papers.title: Where Does Agent Reliability Come From? A Cross-Benchmark Decomposition of Verification Loops, Specialist Models, and Scaffolding in a Production Enterprise Agent

notes.takeaway: First end-to-end instrumentation of a production verification loop, yielding an empirical verifier confusion matrix: across 397 loop-triggering SpreadsheetBench tasks the specialist verifier flagged 8 artifacts (all true errors, zero false alarms), repaired 6, and missed 32 - catch rate c~0.20, fix rate r~0.75, false-alarm rate f~0 - grounding a compounding-reliability model (p' = p(1-fb) + (1-p)cr) in measured parameters. The loop's own telemetry then prices the next investment: raising the catch rate is worth up to +8 pp, raising the fix rate at most +0.5 pp, and the 32 missed errors localize the gap to the neurosymbolic leaderboard leader in the LLM-mediated comparison stage.
notes.why: The branch asks for causal attribution with named systems and real numbers; this delivers a measured operating point for a deployed loop plus a telemetry-driven investment rule, turning the verify-or-scale debate into instrument reading.

papers.title: Proof-or-Stop: Don't Trust the Agent, Trust the Evidence -- Loop Engineering for Verifiable Evidence-Gated Lifecycle Control

notes.takeaway: A named, model-agnostic verified-protocol system for the claim-admissibility problem: lifecycle transitions (reviewed, tested, done, ready-to-merge) advance only on fresh, tracked-source-state-bound, mechanically verifiable evidence, never on agent self-report. Measured in a 9,240-cell powered ablation (hidden-fail amplification cut from 31/1,800 to 2/1,800) and an operated self-application corpus (565 stories, 1,007 review findings, 94.8% resolved).
notes.why: This is exactly the 'verified protocols' strand of the 2026 reliability reckoning: a concrete system with real numbers for deciding which autonomous-agent claims a lifecycle may safely act on, rather than a general appeal to 'add more review'.

papers.title: CAVA: Canonical Action Verification and Attestation for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems

notes.takeaway: Positions itself below Proof-Carrying Agent Actions (PCAA) as the canonical, versioned, hashable action object that a deployer's route-review-prove governance loop operates on, spanning coding hooks, browser automation, payment triggers, and data exports. A 96-seed, 384-variant benchmark shows canonical fingerprinting resists wrapper bypass and approval drift where raw-text and first-token approval binding fail.
notes.why: Names exactly the runtime property this branch tracks for deployment survival: a stable, cross-runtime governance substrate for 'what action was actually approved,' with measured wrapper-bypass and tamper-detection numbers rather than a policy statement alone.

papers.title: Stateful Governance for Concurrent Agentic Systems

notes.takeaway: A runtime architecture for the case where several agents act concurrently on the same shared resources -- budgets, inventory, quotas -- and the governance decision must survive until the effect commits. Provenact sits between the policy engine and the tool call: policy authors write bounded stateful policies over certified policy-state views, providers declare the governed effects and the logical scopes they touch, and a coordinator protects the interval between decision and commit using PostgreSQL transactions and transaction-scoped advisory locks. The prototype is Python with PostgreSQL and SQLite backends and a thin adapter shaped for Microsoft Agent Framework that maps framework function calls into governed action requests, which is the paper's claim to deployability: governed operations pass through the boundary without replacing the surrounding orchestration. Measured against request-local baselines, it removes stale authorization in both a two-agent race and a 256-operation full-conflict workload, and against a global critical section it recovers most of the throughput lost to coarse serialization once governed work takes real time.
notes.why: The branch is about the runtime properties that decide whether demo agents survive deployment, and shared mutable state is where the demo-to-production gap usually opens. A single-agent prototype never sees stale authorization; a fleet of agents sharing a team budget sees it immediately, and the paper shows the standard integration pattern -- pass the current budget as request context, get a decision, then act -- silently produces it. The engineering position is deliberately unambitious in a useful way: no new concurrency primitive, just an explicit contract that makes existing database mechanisms reachable from the governance layer, which is what lets policy stay a first-class reviewable artifact instead of migrating into trusted tool code one guard at a time. The overhead profile is the number to plan against: near parity with a hand-written fixed-policy transaction at zero service time, and 0.93x of it at 10 ms, so the cost of keeping policy first-class is small relative to the cost of serializing everything.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding

notes.takeaway: MSEval grounds 10 collaboration topologies (feature squads, layer specialists, pipeline handoff, swarming, PM oversight, QA-first, PR-style review, adversarial testing, competitive teams, rotation) in real full-stack software delivery with deployment-grounded scoring and cost accounting, rather than abstract communication-pattern simulation.
notes.why: A topology taxonomy tested against actual deployed software rather than a simulated collaboration surface — the foundations branch's 'what a multi-agent system is as a topology' question gets an empirical answer instead of a design-time one.

papers.title: When Agents Coordinate: Measuring Coordination in Multi-Agent AI Coding

notes.takeaway: Represents each of 1,902 coding-agent runs as a temporal network (agents and files as nodes; timestamped, costed messages/reads/writes as edges) to measure coordination directly instead of only task success and cost. Direct messaging grows near-quadratically with team size before leveling off as agents shift to broadcast; shared-spec tasks produce dense teams while pipeline tasks produce sparse, interface-local ones; shared files cut output tokens ~42% at eight agents on message-heavy work; naming a coordinator creates no communication hub and gives no reliable success improvement.
notes.why: A reusable measurement instrument for what a coordination topology actually looks like in practice, complementing this branch's higher-level topology taxonomies with a quantitative network-analysis lens on the same question.

papers.title: Agent-Native Telemetry: Verifiable State-Delta Evidence for Autonomous Operations

notes.takeaway: Structures operational telemetry into signed, hash-chained state-delta primitives with a dual access layer (a compact positional-tuple decoder and a stateful semantic gateway), cutting LLM context tokens by 88.8% and cloud query-scan cost by 96.4% on distributed microservice benchmarks versus OpenTelemetry JSON, with zero successful prompt injections across adversarial trials.
notes.why: Production multi-agent systems are graded on whether they can be operated, not just built; this is a concrete answer to the observability and cost line of that question, with a security property (injection resistance, provable non-occurrence) baked into the wire format rather than bolted on after.

papers.title: Beyond LLM-Based Reasoning: Lightweight GNNs for Agent Failure Attribution

notes.takeaway: Agent failure attribution does not need an LLM. AFANet turns a failed multi-agent trajectory into a turn-level heterogeneous graph -- bidirectional temporal edges between adjacent turns plus same-agent edges linking non-adjacent turns by the same speaker -- with node features concatenating per-conversation TF-IDF/truncated-SVD deviation statistics, positional statistics, and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings. A 2-layer GCN with 65K trainable parameters reaches 74.16 agent-level micro-F1 and 17.42/16.35 pair-level micro/macro-F1 on AEGIS-Bench, which the authors report as top-1 pair-level, and stays highly ranked on the out-of-distribution Who&When set. Training takes 1.1 hours and inference 1.16s in-domain / 0.37s OOD, against 6 to over 74 hours of training and 199-367s of inference for Qwen2.5-7B/14B SFT and SFT+GRPO variants.
notes.why: The frontier theme is the 2026 reliability reckoning, and causal attribution is its first named problem. This is a counter-argument to the assumption that attribution requires a reasoning model: the discriminating signal turns out to be structural -- how a turn deviates from its conversational context and how one agent's contributions cohere over time -- not semantic. Ablations back this: removing the deviation and statistical features drops pair-level micro-F1 from 17.42 to 14.00, a larger hit than removing sentence embeddings, and removing all edges degrades performance across the board.

papers.title: Position: Multi-Agent Systems Should Prioritize Concurrency Control

notes.takeaway: Formalizes the shared substrate rather than describing it. A MAS is n agents with private internal states acting on one shared environment E; every action is classified side-effect-free (a read: reading a file, observing game state, retrieving messages) or side-effecting (a write: writing a file, placing an object, broadcasting a message); and state is split by who may mutate it -- agent-local state (context window, reasoning trace) versus environment state (anything another agent can write). That cut puts a message-passing mailbox on the environment side, not the private side, because other agents write to it. Governance is then two ACID-derived properties over that substrate: consistency, a global property requiring concurrent effects to be mutually compatible, and isolation, an agent-centric property requiring that no agent observe another's incomplete operation sequence, with serializability as its strongest form.
notes.why: This theme asks what a team writes to and who governs it. The paper supplies the vocabulary that answer has been missing: the database isolation hierarchy from Read Uncommitted through Snapshot Isolation to Strict Serializable, applied to blackboard memories, shared repositories, and message buffers. It also names the reason shared memory is harder for agents than for databases -- LLM inference is side-effect-free but runs for seconds to minutes while tool execution finishes in milliseconds, so the window in which another agent can invalidate a read is orders of magnitude wider than classical concurrency control was designed for.

papers.title: The Evaluation Context Protocol (ECP): A Portable Contract for AI Agent Evaluation

notes.takeaway: A vendor-neutral evaluation contract that sits beneath the orchestration frameworks rather than inside one: plain Python, LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI and PydanticAI agents are wrapped by thin adapters that normalize each framework's native notion of intermediate reasoning and tool invocation into a single result object, without rewriting the agent. The adapters differ because the frameworks do (LangChain registers a callback handler, LlamaIndex bridges an async workflow into a synchronous step interface, CrewAI maps a kickoff's task output, PydanticAI extracts from the structured message history it already keeps), and the paper argues their thinness is the evidence that the contract is genuinely separable from the platform. The protocol layer is plain JSON-RPC 2.0, so the SDK and runtime shipped with it are reference implementations rather than mandatory components.
notes.why: This branch tracks the interop protocols stitching coordination patterns together, and ECP's most useful contribution here is the gap it exposes. The repository's two-agent example, a planner and a writer, records the handoffs between them as ordinary tool calls: it works and it is gradeable, but it means a multi-agent system is expressed in the vocabulary of a single agent that happens to call other agents. ECP has no native representation of delegation, and the authors list a delegation identifier that would make multi-agent attribution possible as a plausible addition that would change the shape of the graded surface. Evaluation contracts written for the single-agent case do not extend to teams for free, and attribution is the specific thing that breaks.

papers.title: Adversarial Review: Structured Disagreement for Grounded Agentic Code Review

notes.takeaway: Builds a code-review protocol one design choice at a time on LiveCodeBench (105 stdin-style tasks, 57 hard-tagged), each step motivated by a measured failure of the previous one, with Claude Sonnet 4.5 at medium reasoning throughout. Zero-shot, Self-Refine, single-reviewer and two-reviewers all cluster at 75-77% pass and 34-36 of 57 hard: adding a self-critique that shares the generator's blind spots buys nothing, and a second independent reviewer is within noise of one. MARS breaks the cluster at 82% and 39/57 using five agents (one author, three parallel reviewers, one meta-reviewer). Adversarial Review then beats it at 87% and 43/57 with three agents total and two reviewing roles, a main agent M plus a reviewer R and a critic C that audits R's review. The structural separation is that the inner loop exchanges review text only over a frozen artifact, capped at five rounds, while artifact edits happen only in the outer loop. On SWE-bench Verified, expressed as a pure-text SKILL.md protocol under Claude Code rather than a Python orchestrator, AR reaches 75.2% against 72.6% for MARS and 71.6% zero-shot on all 500 tasks, at roughly 4.5x zero-shot's token cost.
notes.why: The branch's question is when collaborative synergy actually beats coordination overhead, and this is a clean controlled answer on that axis: two interacting reviewing agents outperform four non-interacting ones, and the four cheapest methods are indistinguishable from each other. Scaling agent count is not the lever; constraining the communication channel to a single explicit disagreement exchange is. The worked matplotlib case shows the mechanism concretely, where zero-shot and MARS both patch the caller and re-apply tick visibility after the reset has destroyed it (45 and 50 lines, both failing hidden tests) while the critic catches the reviewer's identical first-round mistake and AR patches the callee in about 20 lines, the only patch that passes.

notes.takeaway: Names and measures a failure mode of cooperative agent systems: agents optimize for agreement rather than correctness. On SWE-PRBench (100 real GitHub PR diffs, F1 over comments matched against human reviewer feedback by a GPT-5.2 judge agreeing with human annotators at Cohen's kappa 0.75), naive AR is the worst of the four methods tested at F1 0.457, below single-reviewer (0.495), MARS (0.501) and two-reviewers (0.503). Two case studies locate why. In over-decomposition, the reviewer hedges, the critic confirms most hedges and adds a speculative bug, and the judge marks 3 of 5 comments fabricated (F1 0.250 on that task). In yielding, the critic raises a real concern, the reviewer rebuts with a file-level argument citing no code, and the critic flips to AGREE, dropping the genuine bug (F1 0.286, against MARS at 0.667 on the same task). The fix is one prompt iteration with no structural change: the critic must choose among three verdicts rather than two, AGREE, DISAGREE EVIDENCE with a code citation that contradicts the flag, or DISAGREE CONCERN for an objection that cannot point to contradicting code, and on a CONCERN the reviewer must cite code in the diff that confirms the bug or drop the flag. That lifts AR to F1 0.533, the highest in the subset.
notes.why: Calibrated consensus is one of this branch's open problems, and here it is with a named system and real numbers on both sides of the fix. The result that matters is not that structured disagreement works but that it does not come for free from the topology: the same R-plus-C structure produces the worst reviews in the field and then the best, with the number of agents and the way they connect unchanged and only the prompts different. Consensus among LLM reviewers is not evidence of correctness unless disagreement is forced to name the code it rests on, and the LiveCodeBench win did not predict the SWE-PRBench behavior, so a protocol validated on code generation cannot be assumed to hold as a review protocol.

papers.title: LongRCA Bench: Diagnosing Responsible Roles and Root Causes in Long-Horizon Agent Failures

notes.takeaway: Causal attribution in multi-agent runs, measured on failures that occurred naturally rather than by injection. The 1,140 trajectories span five agent organizations: diagnosis-execution-verification teams (SWE-bench Pro, Terminal Bench 2), Magentic-One group chat (TravelPlanner), a sequential or planner-critic-action team (VitaBench), and a planner-web-surfer-critic workflow (WebArena Verified), generated by MiniMax-M2.5, Kimi-K2.5 and Qwen3.5-Plus. Twenty-two CS graduate annotators labeled every one, at 30 to 40 minutes each, recording a responsible role, the earliest decisive root-cause step, and a written rationale. The labeling rules are what make the target well-posed across topologies: a repaired earlier error is excluded, a later step that only executes, propagates or exposes an existing error is excluded, and under a handoff the instruction step is selected when it already carries the decisive error and the recipient carries it out unchanged. The role and the step are predicted and scored independently, never inferred from each other. The best result on that target is RCTA at 51.1% role and 24.1% exact step.
notes.why: The frontier branch tracks causal attribution as an open problem now attached to named systems and real numbers, and this is its long-horizon entry. It also sharpens the target: role and step have to be scored separately, because a method that reads the role off the emitter of the step it picked can look competent at attribution while localizing nothing. Practically, it says a 2026 orchestrator running planner-executor-verifier teams has roughly even odds of being told which agent broke a run, and roughly one chance in four of being told where.

papers.title: Candidate supply and answer selection shape the value of LLM judging in multi-agent systems

notes.takeaway: Coordination overhead is priced against what it buys, on 2,450 MedXpertQA questions with 7,350 runs per protocol. A single response scores 39.88% at 1.00x token cost. Five-answer majority voting without any communication reaches 41.06% at 4.96x. An open committee with source-labelled peer review reaches 42.20% at 10.73x, which is +1.14 points over voting (95% CI 0.42 to 1.90). An anonymous evidence board reaches 41.89% at 6.07x, +0.83 points with a CI that includes zero. Meanwhile an oracle that scores a question correct whenever any initial response held the correct answer sits 13.13 to 14.38 points above what the systems actually reported, so the loss is after generation, not during it. Where the plurality initial answer was wrong and an outnumbered correct answer existed, the open committee still reported the popular error in 73.25% of cases and the evidence board in 59.61%. Discussion length does not help: 90.48 to 95.37% of runs converged after a single round across star, complete, ring, and hierarchical topologies, and forcing six full rounds raised token use to 33x-49x without consistent gains.
notes.why: This branch is about when collaborative synergy beats coordination overhead, and here it mostly does not. Doubling the token bill over plain voting bought about one point, and the specific harm is legible: unfiltered peer communication converts a generated minority correct answer into a confidently reported majority error.

notes.takeaway: Judge reliability is a property of the candidate supply, not a fixed trait of the judge. Measured as rank AUC over 15,336 questions, 67,163 pools, and 823,988 candidate pairs, reliability rises sigmoidally with pgen, the fraction of correct candidates in the full bank, completing half its rise above chance at pgen = 14.7% (95% CI 14.3 to 15.1) and falling below 0.5 outright in the lowest-availability group. Holding the displayed pool fixed at 2 correct and 6 wrong candidates preserves the relationship (midpoint 12.2%), so pgen indexes question-level separability rather than how many correct options the judge can see. The midpoint moves to 28.6% on HLE multiple choice and 36.9% on HLE open answer, and two generator settings with identical mean rank AUC (0.8493) produce R-squared of 0.022 and 0.928 against availability. Replaying 81,390 frozen 8-candidate pools changes only the terminal selection rule: majority voting scores 63.82%, rank-power weighting at t = 2 to 4 reaches 70.82 to 70.95%, and top-ranked selection 69.04%. The gain is regime-dependent, +6.02 points when correct candidates are rare, +7.87 at intermediate availability, and -3.22 when correct candidates already dominate the bank.
notes.why: Calibrated consensus with real numbers, including the regime where the calibration hurts. The design isolates the claim properly: the candidate pools are frozen and replayed, so the 7-point gain is attributable to the selection rule alone rather than to more sampling or different communication.

opportunities: Causal failure attribution in agent chains
Pinpoint which agent and step is responsible when a distributed, silent multi-agent failure surfaces — and do it online, at the earliest decisive error, rather than as a post-mortem.
Formally verified coordination protocols
Model agent handoff and coordination protocols in a formal language (e.g. TLA+) and prove — or automatically repair — their safety, importing classical model checking into the agent world.
Token-budget-aware orchestration planner
Plan and execute orchestration under a hard cost ceiling, making budget overruns (double-spend, delegation fanout races) impossible by construction rather than catching them at runtime.
Durable shared team-memory substrate
Build a shared store a team can actively write to, consolidate, type, and prune — one that accumulates competence instead of slop and survives across sessions.
Emergent-behavior evaluation harness
Evaluate the swarm rather than the agent: soft-label, population-level harnesses that measure risks no single agent produces in isolation, since per-agent alignment does not compose.
Information-flow control between agents
Control what evidence and authority flow across agent boundaries so a locally-safe action cannot combine with others into a policy violation, and confidence cannot be weaponized into execution.
Confidence-calibrated consensus
Separate agreement from correctness: principled abstention thresholds and grounded claim typing so a manager never treats an assertive worker report as evidence of truth.
Learned dynamic topology per task
Learn the right communication graph per task and per query difficulty rather than fixing a static dense topology, escaping the average-complexity trap.
Optimal human-checkpoint placement
Place human-in-the-loop checkpoints at exactly the decisions automation provably fails (entity disambiguation, irreversible mutations) without losing the speedup of autonomy.
Replayable agent-trace observability standard
Standardize agent/workflow/tool/model spans and metrics so every reasoning chain is reconstructable — the substrate every other open problem (attribution, eval, cost) depends on.
Cognitive-tier model routing
Route routine decisions to cheap models and escalate to expensive ones only on disagreement or difficulty, controlling cost without sacrificing quality.
Cross-session organizational agent memory
Persist institutional memory — laws, roles, conventions, learned skills — across sessions and users so a team improves over time instead of rediscovering the same workflows and mistakes.
